sections.title: Material comparison — 3 guides
sections.chip: 3 cards stay three · read times out
sections.live: LIVE H2 → Material Comparison · “Compound-level analysis to inform your material specification decisions.” · three read times on three unwritten guides

fields.label: H2 · intro
fields.value: Material Comparison
fields.note: [no change] — and this is the strongest of the three categories: compound selection is the question Margo is asked most and the one the site already answers best

fields.label: Card 1
paragraphs: Compares silicone and EPDM across thermal stability, weathering and fluid compatibility — silicone −60 to +220 °C, EPDM −40 to +140 °C — and the trade-off that decides most specifications: EPDM resists ozone and weather, silicone survives the higher temperature, and neither tolerates mineral oil.
lits:
MATERIAL COMPARISON · 5 min read
Silicone vs EPDM: Selecting the Right Elastomer for High-Temperature Seals
fields.note:
44 words · live is 16 · Updated 2026-09-03 — all seven guides are written, so the three holding changes on this card come off: the read time is published rather than struck, the description is in the present tense because the guide exists, and Read Guide points at the article instead of deflecting to Ask an engineer. The read times are the article sheets’ own figures, not estimates.
The two temperature ranges come from the locked homepage table and cost nothing to state now. The oil sentence is the actual answer to the question — it is the thing a buyer comparing these two compounds most often gets wrong, and putting it on the card means the card is useful even before the guide exists

fields.label: Card 2
paragraphs: Compares fluorocarbon and nitrile across temperature, chemical resistance and cost-in-use — FKM −20 to +250 °C, NBR −30 to +120 °C. FKM is the answer where temperature or aggressive media demand it; NBR is the answer everywhere else, and it costs a fraction as much.
lits:
MATERIAL COMPARISON · 6 min read
FKM vs NBR: Which Rubber Is Right for Your Application?
fields.note: 44 words · live is 15 · “cost-in-use” is the right frame and the live card already has it. The addition states the decision plainly: this comparison is almost always a cost question wearing a technical costume, and saying so is more useful than another spec table

fields.label: Card 3
paragraphs: Sets out a decision framework across the compounds we mix — FKM, NBR, EPDM, silicone and neoprene — with temperature ranges, hardness bands and chemical compatibility, and the flange standards a gasket is drawn to: ASME B16.21 for nonmetallic flat gaskets, EN 1514-1, AWWA C111/A21.11 for water.
lits:
MATERIAL COMPARISON · 8 min read
Gasket Material Selection Guide
fields.note:
49 words · live is 33 · “Includes a material matrix” becomes “will set out” — the live wording promises a document that does not exist.
The three standards are the addition and they are the reason this guide should ship first. All three are verified in this content set, and ASME B16.21 is the correction to an error the live site makes on three pages, where B16.20 — metallic gaskets — is cited for rubber. Publishing this guide fixes a sitewide error and earns a term nobody else is targeting

notes: Card titles are <h3> under the category <h2>. Correct in the live build.

These three are the highest-intent topics on the site. Silicone vs EPDM, FKM vs NBR and gasket material selection are all high-volume, and the comparison format is what answer engines lift most readily.
The figures on the cards do work now. Even unwritten, each card carries an extractable temperature range and a one-sentence decision rule — which is more than most published competitor guides manage.

Link each card to the matching product page as well as the article: gaskets to /products/gaskets, FKM/NBR to /products/o-rings and /products/oil-seals. The article is a placeholder; the product page is not.
No TechArticle schema on cards. The hub describes; the article declares, once it exists.

sections.title: Sizing & spec — 2 guides
sections.live: LIVE H2 → Sizing & Spec · the O-ring card names BS 1806 without noting it has been superseded

fields.label: H2 · intro
fields.value: Sizing & Spec
fields.note: [no change] — and “tolerances” is a word this site needs to get right, since it currently publishes four different tolerance figures across four pages

fields.label: Card 1
paragraphs: Cross-references the international sizing standards with tolerance and groove-dimension guidance. ISO 3601-1 is the current standard and its size code matches the AS568 dash number; BS 1806 was superseded by BS ISO 3601 but is still widely quoted, so a working chart has to carry all three.
leads: ISO 3601-1 is the current standard and its size code matches the AS568 dash number; BS 1806 was superseded by BS ISO 3601 but is still widely quoted
lits: O-Ring Size Chart: AS568, BS1806 & Metric Standards Explained

SIZING & SPEC · 5 min read
O-Ring Size Chart: AS568, ISO 3601-1 and BS 1806 Explained
fields.note:
48 words · live is 14 · the title changes and the reason is a credibility one. BS 1806 has been superseded by BS ISO 3601. It is not wrong to name it — it is still very widely used for cross-reference, which is exactly why it belongs on a chart — but a sizing guide for engineers that names only the withdrawn standard and omits the current one loses the reader it is aimed at.
Naming all three, and saying which is current, is the whole value of the guide and it can be said on the card today. Verified live 2026-09-02. Note the spacing fix too: BS1806 is written BS 1806

fields.label: Card 2
paragraphs: Covers bond geometry, surface preparation and the failure modes that decide whether a bonded part lasts — across the five applications where the bond is the part. No load-rating table: a load rating belongs to a part, not to a bond. We bond in-house — bushes, mounts and bonded seals — so the guide is written from the tooling and the process rather than from a textbook.
lits:
SIZING & SPEC · 7 min read
Rubber-to-Metal Bonded Parts: Design & Specification Guide
fields.note: 40 words · live is 14 · “We bond in-house” is the addition (client-confirmed) and it is what separates this guide from every generic version of it online. Of the seven topics this is the one where Margo has the strongest claim to be the author — the anti-vibration mounts and bushes product pages both depend on the capability

notes: O-ring size chart is the highest-volume term on this entire website and it is a page that gets bookmarked and returned to, which is rare for a manufacturer. It is worth building properly — real tables, not an image — and it is the one guide here that can earn links.
Standard designations are text. AS568, ISO 3601-1, BS 1806 — each is a searched string, and a chart delivered as an image ranks for none of them.
Do not publish a size chart as a PDF download. The site already has 22 dead downloads; this one belongs on the page.
Link card 2 to /products/anti-vibration-mounts and /products/bushes, which carry the bonding detail today.
ISO 3302-1 belongs in card 1’s guide too when it is written — a tolerance guide is the natural home for the class system that replaces the four ± figures published across this site.

fields.label: Card 1
paragraphs: Sets out a due-diligence checklist for quality systems, tooling ownership, capacity and documentation — including the three structural questions that separate a manufacturer from a trading house: who mixes the compound, who owns the tooling, and whose name is on the batch record.
leads: the three structural questions that separate a manufacturer from a trading house: who mixes the compound, who owns the tooling, and whose name is on the batch record.

How to Evaluate a Precision Rubber Manufacturer: 8 Questions to Ask
fields.note:
45 words · live is 14 · the three questions come from the factory-versus-trading-company section already drafted for /about, so most of this guide is written.
One sequencing warning for the developer. A guide telling buyers to “ask for the certificate, then verify it with the issuing body” cannot ship while another page of the same site claims four certifications Margo does not hold. /why-margo comes down before this guide goes up — otherwise the guide indicts its own publisher

fields.label: Card 2
paragraphs: Compares lead time, quality systems, minimum order and total landed cost for procurement managers assessing supply-chain risk.
lits:
SOURCING & BUYER DECISION · 6 min read
India vs China: Sourcing Rubber Seals & Gaskets for Export Markets
fields.note:
18 words · live is 19 · deliberately the shortest card in this sheet.
This is the one topic of the seven where nothing should be added to the card, because everything worth saying needs a source. Duty rates, freight costs, lead times and MOQ norms all move, and every figure would date. Write it from live trade data with dated citations, or do not write it — a comparison piece by an interested party is read sceptically to begin with, and one unsupported number discredits the rest.
Publish this one last, after the five technical guides have established that this library is a reference rather than a sales asset

notes: Card 1 is a strong AEO target. “How do I evaluate a rubber manufacturer?” is asked by procurement teams and answered almost entirely by suppliers marketing themselves; a checklist that names structural tests rather than adjectives is what gets cited.
Card 2 needs dated sources on every figure, and a visible “data as at” line. Without it the guide ages into a liability the way the rest of this site’s unsourced numbers already have.

Do not name competitors or countries pejoratively. A comparison that reads as a sales pitch fails with the procurement audience it targets, and it is the wrong reputation for a library that is otherwise technical.
Card 1 should link to /certifications — a supplier-evaluation guide whose publisher shows its own certificate number, issuer and expiry is making the argument by example.
